chapters.title: Sharding, Partitioning & Consistent Hashing
chapters.summary: How to split data across multiple machines — sharding strategies, consistent hashing internals with virtual nodes, replication topologies, and data rebalancing.

explanation.overview: When a single database can no longer handle the load (data volume, write throughput, or read QPS), you must split (shard/partition) the data across multiple databases. Each shard holds a subset of the data. The challenge: how to split evenly, how to route requests to the correct shard, and what happens when you add/remove shards.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Every request must be routed to the correct shard. A routing function maps a key (user_id, order_id) to a shard. The simplest function is modulo: shard = hash(key) % N. But this breaks badly when N changes — adding 1 shard remaps nearly all keys. Consistent hashing solves this elegantly.

children.title: Sharding Strategies
children.summary: Four approaches to deciding which data goes to which shard.

key_concepts.definition: Assign key ranges to shards: Shard A = users 0-999,999. Shard B = users 1,000,000-1,999,999. PROS: efficient range queries (all user 500,000's data on one shard). Simple to understand and implement. CONS: hot spots — if user 0-999,999 are early adopters who are more active, Shard A gets disproportionate load. New users all go to the latest shard, creating a write hotspot. WHEN TO USE: time-series data (partition by date range — each month on a separate shard), alphabetical partitioning (surnames A-M, N-Z).

shard = hash(key) % num_shards. Distributes data uniformly (assuming a good hash function). PROS: even distribution (no hotspots from key distribution). CONS: range queries are expensive (must query ALL shards and merge results). Adding/removing shards remaps ~all keys — requires massive data migration. WHEN TO USE: even write distribution is the priority, access patterns are key-based (not range-based).

A lookup table (directory) maps each key to its shard. key_id → shard_id stored in a fast lookup service (Redis, ZooKeeper). PROS: maximum flexibility — can move any key to any shard independently. CONS: directory is a single point of failure. Every request must query the directory first (adds latency). WHEN TO USE: when you need fine-grained control over data placement (GDPR — keep EU user data in EU shards).

Shard by geographic region: US users on US-West shard, EU users on EU-Frankfurt shard. Data locality: users are served by the nearest shard, minimizing latency. USED BY: Uber (geo-sharded by city), Spanner (region-based placement). CHALLENGE: users who travel across regions.

children.title: Consistent Hashing — Deep Dive Internals
children.summary: How consistent hashing minimizes data movement when nodes are added/removed — the hash ring, virtual nodes, and real-world implementations.

explanation.overview: Consistent hashing solves the fundamental problem with modulo hashing: when you change the number of servers, modulo remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing guarantees that adding/removing a server only moves K/N keys on average (K = total keys, N = total servers).
explanation.how_it_works_internally: THE HASH RING: Imagine a circular number line from 0 to 2^32 - 1. Both server nodes and keys are hashed onto this ring using the same hash function (MD5, SHA-256, or MurmurHash). Each server occupies a position: hash(server_ip) → position on ring. Each key occupies a position: hash(key) → position on ring. A key is assigned to the FIRST server encountered when walking CLOCKWISE from the key's position. ADDING A NODE: new node N lands between existing nodes A and B. Only keys between A and N (that previously mapped to B) now map to N. All other keys are unaffected. On average, only K/N keys move. REMOVING A NODE: keys that were assigned to the removed node now walk clockwise to the next node. Only that node's keys are affected.

key_concepts.definition: With few physical nodes (3-5), the hash ring has large gaps. One node may own 60% of the ring while another owns 10%. SOLUTION: Virtual Nodes (vNodes) — each physical node creates K virtual nodes on the ring. Instead of hashing just the server IP, hash server_ip + '_0', server_ip + '_1', ..., server_ip + '_K'. With K=150, each physical node has 150 positions spread across the ring. The ring looks uniform even with few physical nodes. Cassandra uses 128-256 vNodes by default. MORE vNODES: finer granularity, more uniform distribution. FEWER: less metadata overhead. ADDED BENEFIT: when a physical node fails, its K virtual nodes' keys are distributed across K different successor nodes (instead of all going to one successor). This prevents cascading overload.

Assign more virtual nodes to powerful servers. A server with 32 GB RAM gets 200 vNodes. A server with 16 GB RAM gets 100 vNodes. This ensures the more powerful server handles proportionally more data.

The hash function must distribute uniformly and be fast. Common choices: MD5 (128-bit, good distribution, slower), MurmurHash3 (128-bit, excellent distribution, very fast — used by Cassandra), xxHash (fastest, used by many modern systems). DO NOT use cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) for consistent hashing — they're unnecessarily slow. Cryptographic properties aren't needed here, only uniform distribution.

Cassandra: consistent hashing with vNodes (num_tokens, default 256). Each node owns tokens on the ring. DynamoDB: consistent hashing with partition key. Redis Cluster: 16384 hash slots (variant of consistent hashing — fixed slots, nodes own slot ranges). Amazon S3: partition keys hashed to distribute objects across storage nodes. Content-addressable storage: hash(content) → store on the corresponding node (dedup-friendly).

children.title: Replication Topologies
children.summary: How data is copied across nodes for fault tolerance and read scalability.

key_concepts.definition: One node (leader/primary) accepts all writes. Changes are replicated to follower nodes (read replicas). Followers handle read queries to distribute read load. INTERNAL: leader writes to WAL → streams WAL records to followers → followers replay WAL. Sync replication: leader waits for at least 1 follower ACK before confirming write (slower, more durable). Async replication: leader confirms immediately, streams later (faster, risk of data loss if leader crashes before replication). PROS: simple, strong consistency from leader, read scalability. CONS: leader is a write bottleneck, failover complexity (picking a new leader, handling divergent state). TOOLS: Postgres streaming replication, MySQL replication, MongoDB replica sets. FAILOVER: Postgres with Patroni — automatic leader election using etcd or ZooKeeper. If leader dies, Patroni promotes the most up-to-date replica. AWS RDS Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover in ~30 seconds.

Multiple nodes accept writes. Each leader replicates to all others asynchronously. ADVANTAGE: writes accepted in any region (low latency for global users). CHALLENGE: write conflicts — two leaders modify the same row simultaneously. Conflict resolution strategies: (1) Last-Write-Wins (LWW) — highest timestamp wins (risk: clock skew loses writes). (2) Application-level — merge function (Git-like merge, CRDTs). (3) Conflict avoidance — route all writes for a given user to one leader (effectively single-leader per user). USED BY: Google Docs (OT/CRDT), CouchDB (conflict resolution with revision trees), active-active database setups.

No designated leader. Any node accepts reads AND writes. Client writes to W nodes simultaneously. Client reads from R nodes and takes the most recent value (by timestamp or version vector). W + R > N guarantees overlap: at least one read node has the latest write (quorum). EXAMPLE: N=3, W=2, R=2. Write goes to 2 of 3 nodes. Read from 2 of 3 nodes. At least 1 overlap → guaranteed to read latest. If W=1, R=3: fast writes (fire-and-forget to 1), slow reads (must read all 3). If W=3, R=1: slow writes (all must ACK), fast reads. TUNABLE PER QUERY: Cassandra's CONSISTENCY LEVEL can be set per query (ONE, QUORUM, ALL). Read repair: if a read finds stale values on some nodes, the coordinator sends the latest value to those nodes. Anti-entropy: background Merkle tree comparison to find and fix inconsistencies. USED BY: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak.

Capture every change in the database (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) and stream it as events to downstream systems. The database's WAL/binlog is treated as an event stream. Tools: Debezium (reads Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog, MongoDB oplog → publishes to Kafka). USE CASES: keep cache in sync (CDC → consumer → cache invalidation), build search index (CDC → consumer → Elasticsearch update), event sourcing from a relational DB, data warehouse sync (CDC → Kafka → ETL → data warehouse).

children.title: Sharding Challenges
children.summary: The hard problems that arise from sharded architectures.

key_concepts.definition: If user data is on Shard A and their orders on Shard B, a JOIN requires fetching from both shards at the application layer. Solutions: (1) Co-locate related data on the same shard (shard everything by user_id). (2) Denormalize — store the user's name in the order record. (3) Use a scatter-gather pattern — query all shards in parallel, merge results. TRADE-OFF: denormalization increases storage and update complexity but eliminates cross-shard queries.

One shard receives disproportionate traffic. Even with hash sharding, highly active keys (celebrity user, viral product) create hotspots. Solutions: (1) Add a random suffix to split hot keys: user_123 → user_123_0, user_123_1, ..., user_123_9 (10 sub-shards). Reads must query all 10 and merge. (2) Dedicated shard for known hot keys. (3) Application-level caching to absorb reads. Instagram's approach: detect hot partitions via monitoring, automatically split them.

When adding new shards, data must be redistributed. Consistent hashing minimizes movement (only K/N keys move). During rebalancing: both old and new locations may have the data — use versioning or routing rules to handle requests during migration. AUTOMATION: Cassandra does this automatically when a node joins (bootstrapping). DynamoDB handles it transparently. Manual sharding (e.g., Postgres + application routing) requires custom migration scripts.

A single business operation spanning multiple shards can't use a local transaction. Options: 2PC (blocking, coordinator SPOF — avoid), Saga pattern (compensating transactions), eventual consistency with reconciliation jobs. INDUSTRY STANDARD: design your shard key so that transactions stay within a single shard (shard by user_id, and user operations only touch one shard).

chapters.title: CAP Theorem, Consensus & Distributed Systems Theory
chapters.summary: CAP/PACELC theorems, Raft consensus internals (leader election, log replication), Paxos, ZooKeeper/etcd, and distributed locking mechanisms.

explanation.overview: These are the theoretical foundations that explain WHY distributed systems must make trade-offs. CAP tells you what's impossible, consensus protocols tell you how to achieve the possible, and distributed locks/coordination services provide building blocks for higher-level patterns.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: In any distributed system with replicated data, you must handle network partitions (they WILL happen in production). CAP forces you to choose between consistency and availability during a partition. Most real systems are more nuanced — PACELC extends the analysis to normal operation.

children.title: CAP Theorem & PACELC
children.summary: What CAP actually means, common misunderstandings, and the more practical PACELC model.

key_concepts.definition: In the presence of a network Partition (P), you must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A). You CANNOT have all three simultaneously. IMPORTANT NUANCE: P is not optional — network partitions always happen in production (switch failure, cable cut, network congestion). So the real choice is: CP or AP during a partition. During NORMAL operation (no partition), you can have both C and A. CP systems: during partition, refuse requests to maintain consistency. MongoDB (primary unavailable = no writes), HBase, ZooKeeper, etcd. AP systems: during partition, continue serving requests with potentially stale data. Cassandra (any node accepts writes, merge later), DynamoDB, CouchDB. COMMON MISCONCEPTION: CAP does not mean you must give up one permanently. You choose behavior DURING a partition. Most of the time (99.99%), there's no partition and both C and A are maintained.

Extends CAP: during Partition, choose Availability or Consistency. ELSE (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. This captures real trade-offs better. PA/EL: highly available during partition, low latency normally (Cassandra, DynamoDB). PC/EC: consistent during partition, consistent normally but higher latency (MongoDB, PostgreSQL with sync replication). PA/EC: available during partition, consistent normally (unusual). PC/EL: consistent during partition, low latency normally (by using quorum reads/writes). EXAMPLE: DynamoDB is PA/EL — during a partition, it stays available (AP). During normal operation, it offers low latency reads from any replica (eventual consistency). You CAN request strong consistency (read from leader) but at higher latency cost.

children.title: Raft Consensus — Deep Dive
children.summary: How Raft achieves consensus in a distributed system — leader election, log replication, and safety guarantees.

explanation.overview: Raft is a consensus protocol designed to be understandable (unlike Paxos). It ensures that a cluster of servers agrees on a sequence of operations, even if some servers crash. Used by: etcd (Kubernetes state store), CockroachDB, TiKV, Consul, HashiCorp Vault.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Raft divides consensus into three sub-problems: leader election, log replication, and safety. At any time, each server is in one of three states: Leader (handles all client requests), Follower (passive, responds to leader), Candidate (trying to become leader).

step_by_step.title: Leader Election
step_by_step.detail: Normal state: one leader, rest are followers. Each follower has an election timeout (randomized, 150-300ms). If a follower doesn't hear from the leader (via heartbeat AppendEntries RPCs) before timeout, it assumes the leader is dead. Follower → increments its term → transitions to Candidate → votes for itself → sends RequestVote RPCs to all other nodes. Each node votes for at most one candidate per term (first-come-first-served). If candidate receives votes from a majority (N/2 + 1), it becomes the new Leader. If no majority (split vote), all candidates' election timers expire with new random timeouts, and election restarts. The randomized timeout makes split votes rare (typically resolved in 1-2 rounds). TERM: monotonically increasing integer. Acts as a logical clock. A server with a higher term supersedes servers with lower terms. If a server receives a message with a higher term, it immediately becomes a follower.

step_by_step.title: Log Replication
step_by_step.detail: Client sends a command to the leader. Leader appends the command to its log as a new entry (with term and index). Leader sends AppendEntries RPCs to all followers with the new entry. When a majority of followers have appended the entry, it's 'committed'. Leader applies committed entries to its state machine and responds to client. Followers apply committed entries to their state machines in order. If a follower's log diverges (missed entries), the leader sends all missing entries. The leader never deletes or modifies its log — only appends.

step_by_step.title: Safety Guarantees
step_by_step.detail: Election Restriction: a candidate must have a log at least as up-to-date as a majority of nodes to win an election. This ensures the new leader has all committed entries. Leader Completeness: if an entry is committed in a given term, it will be present in the logs of all leaders for higher terms. No Split Brain: at most one leader per term (each node votes once per term, leader needs majority). A CLUSTER OF 5 NODES tolerates 2 failures. A cluster of 3 tolerates 1 failure. General: 2F+1 nodes to tolerate F failures.

configurable_params.name: election-timeout
configurable_params.effect: Lower = faster leader election. Higher = fewer unnecessary elections during network jitter.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Too low: frequent elections in lossy networks. Too high: longer unavailability after leader crash. Must be >> heartbeat interval.

configurable_params.name: heartbeat-interval
configurable_params.effect: How often leader sends empty AppendEntries to prevent follower timeouts.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Lower = faster failure detection but more network traffic. Rule: election_timeout ≈ 10× heartbeat_interval.

children.title: ZooKeeper, etcd & Coordination Services
children.summary: Distributed coordination services used for leader election, config management, and distributed locking.

key_concepts.definition: Centralized coordination service by Apache. Data model: hierarchical namespace of znodes (like a filesystem: /services/api/leader). Each znode holds small data (< 1 MB) and has a version number. Znode types: Persistent (survives client disconnect), Ephemeral (auto-deleted when creating client's session ends — used for leader election and service discovery), Sequential (append incrementing number: /locks/lock-0000000001). WATCHES: clients register watchers on znodes — notified when the znode changes. One-time trigger (must re-register after notification). Used for: leader election (create ephemeral znode /leader — first to create wins, others watch and take over when it's deleted), distributed locks (sequential ephemeral znodes — lowest sequence number holds lock), configuration management (all services watch /config, get notified on change), service discovery (services create ephemeral znodes under /services/api; clients read the list). INTERNAL: ZAB (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast) protocol — similar to Raft. One leader, followers. Leader processes all writes, followers handle reads. Requires majority quorum (3 or 5 nodes).

Distributed key-value store using Raft consensus. Foundation of Kubernetes — stores all cluster state (pods, services, configs, secrets). Key differences from ZooKeeper: gRPC API (vs ZooKeeper's custom protocol), flat key-space with prefix queries (vs ZooKeeper's hierarchical znodes), persistent watches (vs ZooKeeper's one-time watches), leases (TTL-based keys, similar to ephemeral znodes). Used for: Kubernetes cluster state, service discovery (with etcd + CoreDNS), distributed locking (etcd lease + comparison), leader election (etcd election campaign). PERFORMANCE: ~10K writes/sec, ~100K reads/sec per cluster. Data should be < 8 GB (it's for metadata, not bulk data).

children.title: Distributed Locking
children.summary: Mechanisms for mutual exclusion across distributed systems — Redis locks, Redlock, ZooKeeper locks, and fencing tokens.

key_concepts.definition: Simplest distributed lock: SET lock_key unique_value NX PX 30000 (set if not exists, expire in 30 seconds). If SETNX returns OK, you hold the lock. Release: Lua script that checks if the value matches (prevents releasing someone else's lock). PROBLEM: if Redis restarts (no persistence) or network partition occurs, the lock is lost. Two clients can hold the 'same lock'. Acceptable for: efficiency locks (dedup, cache population) where occasional double-processing is tolerable. NOT acceptable for: correctness locks (payment processing, inventory deduction).

Martin Kleppmann's criticism notwithstanding, Redlock is Redis's attempt at a stronger distributed lock. ALGORITHM: run 5 independent Redis instances. To acquire: SET on all 5 with unique_value and TTL. If majority (3+) succeed within the TTL time - clock drift, lock is acquired. Release: DEL on all 5. PROBLEM: relies on wall-clock time assumptions. If a server's clock jumps forward (NTP correction, VM pause), the lock can expire on some nodes while the client still thinks it holds it. Martin Kleppmann argument: Redlock is fundamentally unsafe for correctness because it depends on timing assumptions that can't be guaranteed.

CREATE SEQUENTIAL EPHEMERAL ZNODE: /locks/resource-0000000047. Read all children of /locks/. If your znode has the LOWEST sequence number → you hold the lock. If not → watch the znode with the next lower sequence number. When it's deleted (lock released or client died), check again. WHY THIS WORKS: ephemeral znodes auto-delete on client death (session timeout). No zombie locks. Sequential ordering prevents thundering herd (each waiter watches only its predecessor, not all predecessors). ZooKeeper's consensus guarantees the ordering is consistent.

Even with a correct lock, a client can hold a lock, pause (GC pause, VM snapshot), and resume after the lock expired — now it and a new lock holder both think they hold the lock. SOLUTION: when a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token (e.g., 42). The client sends this token with every write to the protected resource. The resource rejects writes with a token lower than the highest it's seen. If client A pauses with token 42, lock expires, client B gets token 43, client A wakes up and tries to write with token 42 → REJECTED (43 > 42). This is the only way to make distributed locks truly safe for correctness. etcd lease IDs serve as fencing tokens.

Martin Kleppmann — How to do Distributed Locking

chapters.title: Message Queues, Streams & Event-Driven Patterns
chapters.summary: Complete guide to async communication — Kafka internals (partitions, offsets, ISR, leader election, KRaft), RabbitMQ exchanges, SQS, event-driven patterns (Event Sourcing, CQRS, Outbox, Saga), and when to use each.

explanation.overview: In a monolithic application, components call each other directly via function calls. In a distributed system with microservices, direct synchronous calls create tight coupling, cascading failures, and throughput bottlenecks. Message queues and event streams decouple producers from consumers, enable asynchronous processing, and absorb traffic spikes. This is one of the most important topics in system design — nearly every large-scale system uses some form of async messaging.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: At its core, a message queue is a FIFO buffer: producers write messages, consumers read them. The queue persists messages until they're consumed. The key difference between a 'message queue' (RabbitMQ, SQS) and a 'streaming platform' (Kafka) is that queues deliver each message to ONE consumer (point-to-point) and remove it after consumption, while streams retain messages in an ordered log and allow multiple consumer groups to independently read at their own pace.

children.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
children.summary: Why async communication matters and when to use sync (HTTP/gRPC) vs async (queue/stream).

explanation.overview: Synchronous (request-response): Service A calls Service B and WAITS for a response before continuing. Example: user clicks 'Place Order' → Order Service synchronously calls Payment Service → waits for payment result → returns to user. Pros: simple, immediate feedback. Cons: if Payment Service is slow (2 seconds) or down, the user waits or gets an error. Caller and callee are tightly coupled — both must be available simultaneously. Asynchronous (fire-and-forget or event-driven): Service A publishes a message/event and continues immediately without waiting. Example: user clicks 'Place Order' → Order Service writes order to DB, publishes 'OrderCreated' event to Kafka → returns 'Order received' to user immediately → Payment Service consumes the event and processes payment in the background → notifies user via email/push when payment completes.

key_concepts.definition: Use synchronous calls when: (1) The caller NEEDS the result immediately to continue (validating a credit card number, fetching user profile to display). (2) The operation is fast (< 100ms). (3) Failure must be communicated to the user immediately. (4) The two services are in the same trust boundary and low latency path.

Use asynchronous messaging when: (1) The operation is slow (video transcoding, email sending, PDF generation). (2) The caller doesn't need the result immediately (order confirmation email). (3) You need to absorb traffic spikes (100K orders/minute during flash sale → queue absorbs, workers process at steady rate). (4) You need to decouple services (Order Service shouldn't break if Email Service is down). (5) You need fan-out (one event consumed by multiple services: analytics, notification, billing).

When the consumer can't keep up with the producer. In sync: the caller gets timeouts or 503s. In async: the queue grows. Back pressure strategies: (1) Queue size limit with rejection (producer gets 'queue full' error). (2) Rate limiting producers. (3) Auto-scaling consumers. (4) Dropping low-priority messages. Kafka handles back pressure naturally — consumers pull at their own pace, and Kafka retains messages based on retention policy (7 days by default).

children.title: Apache Kafka — Deep Dive Internals
children.summary: How Kafka achieves millions of messages/sec — its internal log structure, partition-based parallelism, replication with ISR, and the new KRaft consensus mode.

explanation.overview: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant, real-time data pipelines. Unlike traditional message queues that delete messages after consumption, Kafka retains messages in an ordered, immutable, append-only log. Consumers track their position (offset) and can re-read historical data. This log-based design is what makes Kafka fundamentally different and powerful.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: A Kafka cluster consists of multiple brokers (servers). Data is organized into topics. Each topic is divided into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of records, physically stored as a segment of log files on disk. Producers choose which partition to write to. Consumers read from partitions using offsets.

children.title: Topics, Partitions & Offsets
children.summary: How Kafka organizes data into topics and partitions, and how offsets track consumer position.

explanation.overview: A Topic is a logical category (like 'orders', 'user-events', 'page-views'). Each topic is split into one or more Partitions — each partition is an independent ordered log stored on a single broker. Partitions enable parallelism: with 12 partitions, up to 12 consumers can read in parallel.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: PRODUCING: When a producer sends a message, it must choose a partition. Three strategies: (1) Round-robin — distribute messages across partitions evenly (best throughput). (2) Key-based — hash(message_key) % num_partitions. All messages with the same key go to the same partition, guaranteeing ordering for that key. Example: hash(user_id) ensures all events for user 123 go to partition 7 in order. (3) Custom partitioner — application logic decides. OFFSET: Each message within a partition gets a monotonically increasing offset (0, 1, 2, ...). This is the message's unique ID within its partition. Consumers track their 'current offset' — the last message they've processed. Offsets are stored in a special internal topic: __consumer_offsets (log-compacted). CONSUMING: Consumers pull messages from Kafka (not pushed). A consumer group assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. With 12 partitions and 3 consumers: each consumer reads 4 partitions. If a consumer dies, its partitions are rebalanced to surviving consumers. You can NEVER have more consumers than partitions in a group — extra consumers sit idle. ORDERING GUARANTEE: Messages within a single partition are strictly ordered. NO ordering guarantee across partitions. So if you need global ordering, use 1 partition (sacrifices parallelism) or key-based partitioning for per-key ordering.

key_concepts.definition: Start with: partitions = max(expected_throughput_MB_per_sec / 10, expected_consumer_count). Each partition can handle ~10 MB/s writes. Too few partitions = throughput bottleneck. Too many = more file handles, longer leader elections, more memory on brokers. Industry practice: start with 6-12 partitions, increase later if needed. WARNING: increasing partitions is easy; decreasing is impossible without recreating the topic.

When consumers join/leave a group, Kafka reassigns partitions. During rebalancing (which takes seconds to minutes), consumption pauses. Strategies: (1) Eager rebalancing (default in older versions) — revoke all partitions, reassign all. Causes full stop-the-world. (2) Cooperative rebalancing (incremental, Kafka 2.4+) — only revoke affected partitions. Much shorter disruption. CONFIGURABLE: session.timeout.ms = time before Kafka considers a consumer dead (default 45s). heartbeat.interval.ms = how often consumer sends heartbeat (default 3s, must be < session.timeout/3).

configurable_params.name: num.partitions
configurable_params.effect: More partitions = more parallelism but more overhead.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Rule: partitions ≥ consumer instances. Start with 6-12. Can't decrease later.

configurable_params.name: retention.ms
configurable_params.effect: How long messages are retained. After this, they're eligible for deletion.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Longer retention = more disk. Shorter = risk of data loss if consumers fall behind.

configurable_params.name: max.message.bytes
configurable_params.effect: Maximum size of a single message.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Large messages reduce throughput and increase latency. For large payloads, use claim check pattern — store data in S3 and pass the S3 URL in the message.

children.title: Replication, ISR & Leader Election
children.summary: How Kafka replicates data for durability and performs leader election when brokers fail.

explanation.overview: Each partition has multiple replicas distributed across different brokers. One replica is the Leader (handles all reads and writes), and the rest are Followers (passively replicate the leader's log). This provides fault tolerance — if the leader broker crashes, a follower is promoted to leader.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: REPLICATION FLOW: (1) Producer sends message to the partition's Leader broker. (2) Leader appends message to its local log. (3) Followers pull the message from the leader and append to their logs. (4) When all ISR (In-Sync Replicas) have acknowledged, the message is 'committed'. (5) Only committed messages are visible to consumers. ISR (IN-SYNC REPLICAS): The set of replicas that are 'caught up' with the leader — their log end offset is within replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s) of the leader's. If a follower falls behind (slow network, disk issue), it's removed from ISR. When it catches up, it's added back. KEY SETTING: min.insync.replicas (default 1). If set to 2, the producer must receive acknowledgment from at least 2 ISR members before the write is considered successful. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 and replication.factor=3: the write succeeds as long as 2 out of 3 replicas are in sync. If only 1 is in sync, the write fails (NotEnoughReplicasException) — preventing data loss at the cost of availability. LEADER ELECTION: A special broker called the Controller monitors all broker health via heartbeats. When a leader broker fails: (1) Controller detects the failure. (2) Controller selects a new leader from the ISR list (the replica with the most recent data). (3) Controller updates the cluster metadata and notifies all brokers. (4) Clients (producers and consumers) query metadata and redirect to the new leader. Leadership transfer takes 5-30 seconds depending on controller responsiveness and number of affected partitions. UNCLEAN LEADER ELECTION (unclean.leader.election.enable, default false): if ALL ISR replicas are down and only out-of-sync replicas remain, should Kafka elect one? If yes (true): data loss (messages acknowledged to ISR but not replicated to the now-elected leader are lost). If no (false): the partition stays offline until an ISR replica comes back. Choose based on your durability requirements — financial systems = false. Log analytics = true.

key_concepts.definition: Historically, Kafka used Apache ZooKeeper for controller election, broker registration, and cluster metadata. Problems: ZooKeeper is a separate system to manage, limits scaling (ZooKeeper bottlenecks with millions of partitions), and adds operational complexity. KRaft (Kafka Raft) replaces ZooKeeper entirely. A quorum of controller nodes (typically 3) manages cluster metadata using the Raft consensus protocol. Metadata is stored in a Kafka internal topic (__cluster_metadata). Benefits: simplified operations (no more ZooKeeper), faster controller failover (seconds vs minutes), support for millions of partitions. As of Kafka 3.6+, KRaft is production-ready and ZooKeeper is deprecated.

acks=0: producer doesn't wait for any acknowledgment. Fire-and-forget. Fastest but messages can be lost. Use for: metrics/logs where loss is acceptable. acks=1: producer waits for leader acknowledgment only. If leader crashes after ack but before replication, message is lost. Use for: most general workloads (balanced speed and durability). acks=all (or -1): producer waits for ALL ISR replicas to acknowledge. Slowest but strongest durability. Combined with min.insync.replicas=2, provides strong durability guarantee. Use for: financial transactions, critical events.

configurable_params.name: replication.factor
configurable_params.effect: Number of copies of each partition. Industry standard: 3.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Higher = more durability + more disk usage + higher write latency. 3 is the universal standard — can survive 1 broker failure with no data loss.

configurable_params.name: min.insync.replicas
configurable_params.effect: Minimum ISR count for acks=all writes to succeed.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Set to 2 with replication.factor=3 for strong durability. Setting equal to replication.factor means writes fail if ANY replica is down.

configurable_params.name: replica.lag.time.max.ms
configurable_params.effect: If a follower hasn't fetched from leader within this time, it's removed from ISR.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Lower = faster detection of slow replicas but more ISR churn. Higher = more tolerant of temporary network blips.

children.title: Delivery Semantics — At-Most-Once, At-Least-Once, Exactly-Once
children.summary: The three delivery guarantees in messaging systems and how Kafka achieves exactly-once processing.

explanation.overview: Every messaging system must choose among three delivery semantics. The choice fundamentally affects your system's correctness.

key_concepts.definition: A message is delivered zero or one times. It may be lost but never duplicated. Implementation: producer sends message with acks=0 (fire-and-forget) or consumer commits offset BEFORE processing. If consumer crashes after commit but before processing, the message is skipped on restart. Use for: metrics, logs, analytics where losing a few data points is acceptable.

A message is delivered one or more times. It's never lost but may be duplicated. Implementation: producer retries on failure (retries=MAX_INT, acks=all). Consumer processes message FIRST, then commits offset. If consumer crashes after processing but before commit, the message is re-processed on restart. This is the DEFAULT behavior in most Kafka setups. The consumer must be idempotent — processing the same message twice should produce the same result. Example idempotent operation: SET user_balance = 100 (always results in 100). NOT idempotent: INCREMENT user_balance BY 50 (double-processing adds 100).

A message is delivered and processed exactly once. No loss, no duplication. This is the hardest guarantee and most systems don't need it. How Kafka achieves it: (1) Idempotent Producer (enable.idempotence=true): Kafka assigns each producer a PID (producer ID) and each message a sequence number. If a retry sends the same message again, the broker detects the duplicate via PID+sequence and silently drops it. This gives exactly-once WITHIN a single partition. (2) Kafka Transactions (transactional.id=my-app): wraps produce + consumer offset commit into an atomic transaction. Either ALL messages are produced AND offsets committed, or NONE are. The consumer reads with isolation.level=read_committed to only see committed transactional messages. Use for: stream processing (read from topic A → process → write to topic B) where duplicates are unacceptable. TRADE-OFF: transactions add latency (~50-100ms per batch) and reduce throughput by ~20-30%. Most applications don't need exactly-once — at-least-once with idempotent consumers is simpler and sufficient.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When you need at-least-once delivery but your processing isn't naturally idempotent
advanced_tweaks.how: Store a deduplication table (message_id → processed_at) in your database. Before processing, check if message_id exists. If yes, skip. If no, process and insert. Use a unique message ID from the producer (UUID or partition+offset). Wrap the check + process + insert in a database transaction. This gives you exactly-once processing semantics without Kafka transactions.

advanced_tweaks.technique: Outbox Pattern for reliable event publishing
advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When a service must write to DB AND publish an event, and both must succeed or both fail
advanced_tweaks.how: Instead of writing to DB and then publishing to Kafka (which can fail between the two), write to DB AND insert into an 'outbox' table in the SAME database transaction. A separate relay process (or CDC via Debezium) reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka. If publishing fails, it retries from the outbox. This guarantees: if DB write succeeds, the event will eventually be published.

children.title: RabbitMQ vs Kafka vs SQS — When to Use Each
children.summary: Detailed comparison of the three most common messaging systems with concrete guidance on when to use each.

explanation.overview: These three systems are often confused but serve different use cases. The key differences are in message retention, delivery model, ordering guarantees, and operational complexity.

key_concepts.definition: Traditional message broker implementing AMQP protocol. ARCHITECTURE: Producers → Exchange → Queue → Consumer. Exchanges route messages to queues based on rules. Exchange types: Direct (exact routing key match), Fanout (broadcast to all bound queues), Topic (pattern-based routing like 'order.*.created'), Headers (match on message headers). DELIVERY MODEL: Push-based — broker pushes messages to consumers. Smart broker, dumb consumer. Message acknowledged then deleted. No replay capability. ORDERING: Guaranteed within a single queue (FIFO). Not guaranteed across queues. THROUGHPUT: ~20K-50K messages/sec per node (depends on persistence and message size). Much lower than Kafka. PERSISTENCE: messages can be durable (written to disk) or transient (memory only). STRENGTHS: Complex routing rules (topic exchange with wildcards), per-message acknowledgment, priority queues, TTL per message, delayed message delivery. USE WHEN: task queues (background jobs with different priorities), complex routing logic ('route all European orders to EU payment processor queue'), RPC-style request/reply patterns.

Distributed event streaming platform. ARCHITECTURE: Producers → Topic (partitioned log) → Consumer Groups. No routing logic — producers choose a partition, consumers read from assigned partitions. DELIVERY MODEL: Pull-based — consumers pull messages at their own pace. Dumb broker, smart consumer. Messages are retained for a configurable period (default 7 days) regardless of consumption. Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic independently — each at their own offset. ORDERING: Guaranteed within a partition. Per-key ordering with key-based partitioning. THROUGHPUT: ~100K-1M+ messages/sec per broker. Orders of magnitude higher than RabbitMQ. Optimized for sequential disk I/O (append-only writes, OS page cache). REPLAY: consumers can seek to any offset and re-process historical data. This is impossible with RabbitMQ/SQS. STRENGTHS: massive throughput, event replay, log compaction (keep latest value per key), stream processing (Kafka Streams, ksqlDB), exactly-once transactions. USE WHEN: high-throughput event streaming (clickstream, logs, IoT telemetry), event sourcing, real-time data pipelines, any scenario where you need to replay events or have multiple independent consumers.

Fully managed message queue by AWS. Two types: Standard (best-effort ordering, at-least-once delivery, nearly unlimited throughput) and FIFO (strict ordering by message group ID, exactly-once, 3000 messages/sec with batching). DELIVERY MODEL: Pull-based. Message becomes 'invisible' when a consumer receives it (visibility timeout, default 30 seconds). If not deleted within timeout, it reappears for another consumer. After a configurable number of receives (maxReceiveCount), message goes to Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). NO message replay — deleted after successful consumption. STRENGTHS: zero operations (fully managed by AWS), auto-scaling (never worry about provisioning), DLQ built-in, integrates with Lambda (event-driven processing), extremely reliable. USE WHEN: simple async task processing in AWS (send email on order, process image upload), you want zero operational overhead, workloads that don't need replay or complex routing. LIMITATIONS: max message size 256 KB (use S3 for larger payloads with claim check pattern), no routing logic (one queue = one consumer type).

pros: Kafka: highest throughput, replay, multiple consumers
RabbitMQ: flexible routing, priority queues, mature ecosystem
SQS: zero ops, infinite scale, DLQ built-in
cons: Kafka: complex operations, steep learning curve, overkill for simple tasks
RabbitMQ: lower throughput, no replay, operational burden
SQS: AWS lock-in, no replay, limited ordering (FIFO capped at 3K/sec)
tradeoffs.when_to_use: Kafka for high-throughput event streaming and replay. RabbitMQ for complex routing and task queues. SQS for simple AWS-native async processing.
tradeoffs.when_to_avoid: Kafka for simple job queues (<1K/sec). RabbitMQ for >100K messages/sec. SQS when you need message replay or non-AWS deployment.

children.title: Event-Driven Architecture Patterns
children.summary: Advanced patterns for building event-driven systems — Event Sourcing, CQRS, Transactional Outbox, and Saga for distributed transactions.

explanation.overview: These patterns appear in almost every Staff/Principal-level system design interview. They solve the fundamental challenges of data consistency, service decoupling, and audit trails in distributed systems.

children.title: Event Sourcing
children.summary: Instead of storing current state, store the complete history of state changes as an immutable sequence of events.

explanation.overview: Traditional: store the current state (account_balance = $500). Event Sourcing: store every event that led to the current state (deposited $1000, withdrew $300, deposited $200, withdrew $400 → balance = $500). The current state is derived by replaying all events.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Events are immutable facts stored in an append-only log (event store). Each event has: event_id, aggregate_id (the entity it belongs to, e.g., account_123), event_type (AccountCredited, AccountDebited), timestamp, and payload (amount, description). To get the current state: load all events for aggregate_id, replay them in order, accumulate state. This is called 'rehydration'. For performance, periodically save snapshots (current state at event offset N). To rehydrate: load latest snapshot + replay events after snapshot offset. WHY: (1) Complete audit trail — you know exactly what happened and when (regulatory compliance, financial systems). (2) Time travel — reconstruct state at any point in time. (3) Debug by replaying events. (4) No destructive updates — events are never modified or deleted. (5) Easy to add new read models by replaying events through a new projection. TRADEOFF: Complexity — querying the current state is harder (must replay or use projections). Schema evolution is tricky (events are immutable; old events follow old schemas). Eventual consistency between event store and projections.

examples.title: Banking Example
examples.description: Events: [{type: 'AccountOpened', balance: 0}, {type: 'Deposited', amount: 1000}, {type: 'Withdrew', amount: 200}, {type: 'Deposited', amount: 500}]. Current balance = 0 + 1000 - 200 + 500 = $1300. If auditor asks 'what happened on March 5?', filter events by timestamp.

use_cases.why: Regulatory requirement to maintain complete transaction history. Event sourcing provides a natural audit log.
Track every add/remove/quantity change. Can analyze abandonment patterns by replaying cart events.
Git IS event sourcing — each commit is an immutable event. The working directory is derived by replaying commits.

children.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
children.summary: Separate the write path (commands) from the read path (queries), allowing each to be independently optimized and scaled.

explanation.overview: In a traditional CRUD system, the same database model handles both writes and reads. This creates conflicts: writes want normalized data (3NF) for consistency; reads want denormalized data for fast queries. CQRS separates them: the WRITE side (Command Model) handles mutations through commands (CreateOrder, UpdateInventory) and stores data in a write-optimized format (normalized relational DB, event store). The READ side (Query Model) handles queries and stores data in precomputed, denormalized read models optimized for specific query patterns (Elasticsearch for search, Redis for feeds, materialized views for dashboards).
explanation.how_it_works_internally: WRITE flow: Client → Command Handler → validate business rules → persist to write DB → publish event (OrderCreated). READ flow: Event Consumer → update read model(s) → Client queries read model directly. The read models are eventually consistent with the write model (delay of milliseconds to seconds). Multiple read models can exist for different query patterns: read model 1 in Elasticsearch for full-text search, read model 2 in Redis sorted set for leaderboards, read model 3 in Postgres materialized view for analytics dashboards. WHEN TO USE: (1) Read patterns differ significantly from write patterns. (2) Read and write loads are asymmetric (10:1 or higher). (3) You need different storage technologies for different query types. (4) Often combined with Event Sourcing — events from the event store are projected into read models. WHEN NOT TO USE: simple CRUD with similar read/write patterns and modest scale. CQRS adds complexity (two models to maintain, eventual consistency to handle).

use_cases.why: Write model: normalized relational DB for product CRUD. Read model 1: Elasticsearch for search with filters. Read model 2: Redis for 'frequently bought together' recommendations. Read model 3: denormalized JSON in CDN for product detail pages.
Write model: Postgres for posts (user_id, content, timestamp). Read model: Redis sorted set per user containing their precomputed feed — tweets from people they follow, sorted by time.

children.title: Saga Pattern — Distributed Transactions Without 2PC
children.summary: A sequence of local transactions across services, where each step has a compensating action for rollback.

explanation.overview: In a microservice architecture, a single business operation (placing an order) may span multiple services (Order Service, Inventory Service, Payment Service, Shipping Service). You can't use a database transaction across service boundaries. 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) is an option but it's slow, blocking, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The Saga pattern breaks the operation into a sequence of local transactions. If any step fails, previously completed steps are undone via compensating transactions.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: EXAMPLE — Place Order Saga: Step 1: Order Service creates order (status: PENDING). Step 2: Inventory Service reserves items. Step 3: Payment Service charges credit card. Step 4: Order Service confirms order (status: CONFIRMED). Step 5: Shipping Service schedules delivery. If Step 3 (payment) fails: Compensate Step 2: Inventory Service releases reserved items. Compensate Step 1: Order Service marks order as FAILED. TWO STYLES: (1) Choreography: each service publishes events and other services react. Order Service publishes OrderCreated → Inventory Service subscribes, reserves items, publishes ItemsReserved → Payment Service subscribes, charges card, publishes PaymentCompleted → Order Service subscribes, confirms order. No central coordinator. Each service knows its own business logic. PROS: loosely coupled. CONS: hard to trace the flow, hard to debug, circular dependencies can emerge. (2) Orchestration: a central Saga Orchestrator sends commands to each service and handles responses. Orchestrator → 'Reserve items' → Inventory Service → 'Items reserved' → Orchestrator → 'Charge card' → Payment Service → 'Payment failed' → Orchestrator → 'Release items' → Inventory Service. PROS: clear flow, easy to debug, centralized error handling. CONS: orchestrator is a SPOF, tight coupling to orchestrator. INDUSTRY STANDARD: Use orchestration for complex sagas (>3 steps) and choreography for simple ones (2-3 steps). Temporal.io and AWS Step Functions are popular orchestration frameworks.

use_cases.why: Spans order, inventory, payment, shipping services. Each has its own DB. Saga ensures all steps complete or all are rolled back.
Book flight + hotel + car rental across different provider APIs. If hotel booking fails, cancel the flight booking (compensating transaction).

chapters.title: Concurrency & Synchronization
chapters.summary: Concurrency primitives (mutex, semaphore, spinlock, RW-lock), Java memory model, concurrency patterns (producer-consumer, reactor), deadlock detection, and distributed transactions.

explanation.overview: Concurrency is about multiple operations executing in overlapping time periods. Parallelism is about executing simultaneously on multiple cores. In system design, concurrency appears at every level: multiple threads handling requests, multiple servers processing jobs, multiple database clients competing for rows. Understanding concurrency primitives lets you reason about race conditions, deadlocks, and correctness.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: At the CPU level, a single core can only execute one instruction at a time. The OS scheduler rapidly switches between threads (context switch ~1-10µs), creating the illusion of simultaneous execution. On multi-core CPUs, true parallelism occurs. The challenge: when multiple threads access shared mutable state without synchronization, you get race conditions — the result depends on unpredictable timing.

key_concepts.definition: Binary lock: owned by one thread at a time. Other threads calling lock() are put to sleep (blocked) by the OS until the owner calls unlock(). INTERNAL: on Linux, mutex uses futex (fast userspace mutex). The fast path (no contention) is a single atomic CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instruction in userspace — no kernel involvement (~25ns). Only on contention does it syscall into the kernel to sleep the thread. Reentrant mutex: the same thread can acquire it multiple times (maintains a count, must release same number of times). USE: protecting shared data structures (hash maps, queues, counters).

Counter-based synchronization. Initialized with count N. acquire() decrements count. If count < 0, thread blocks. release() increments count. If a thread is waiting, wake it. Binary semaphore (N=1) ≈ mutex but not owned by any thread (any thread can release). Counting semaphore (N>1): limit concurrent access. EXAMPLE: connection pool of 10 connections — semaphore(10). Each thread acquires before using a connection, releases after.

Loop (spin) checking a flag via atomic CAS until it succeeds. Does NOT put the thread to sleep — wastes CPU cycles while waiting. WHEN TO USE: only when the critical section is very short (< 1µs) and context switch cost (1-10µs) exceeds expected wait time. Linux kernel uses spinlocks for short sections where sleeping is not allowed (interrupt handlers). NEVER use in application code for long waits.

Atomic CPU instruction: CAS(addr, expected, new) — if *addr == expected, set *addr = new and return true. Otherwise return false. Foundation of all lock-free data structures. Java AtomicInteger.compareAndSet(), C++ std::atomic. LOCK-FREE COUNTER: instead of mutex { counter++ }, do: loop { old = counter; if CAS(counter, old, old+1) break; }. No blocking, no sleeping — if another thread modified counter between read and CAS, CAS fails and we retry. ABA problem: value changes A→B→A and CAS can't detect it. FIX: use versioned CAS (AtomicStampedReference in Java).

Allows multiple concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. Readers don't block other readers (shared mode), but a writer blocks all readers and writers (exclusive mode). USE: read-heavy data structures (config, caches read 100× more than written). INTERNAL: maintains reader_count + writer flag. reader.lock(): if no writer, increment reader_count. writer.lock(): wait for reader_count=0 and no other writer. STARVATION: writers can starve if readers keep arriving. FIX: fair RW lock (writers get priority after waiting).

Producers put items into a bounded buffer (BlockingQueue). Consumers take items from the buffer. Buffer decouples production rate from consumption rate. INTERNAL: BlockingQueue uses a mutex + two condition variables (not_empty, not_full). put(): lock → if full, wait(not_full) → insert → signal(not_empty) → unlock. take(): lock → if empty, wait(not_empty) → remove → signal(not_full) → unlock. Java: ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue. USE: request processing (web server puts requests in queue, worker threads consume), Kafka consumer pattern.

Pre-create a fixed number of threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue; idle threads pick up tasks. Prevents thread explosion (creating a new thread per request = 10K threads = excessive context switching + OOM). Java: ExecutorService with ThreadPoolExecutor(coreSize, maxSize, keepAlive, queue). CONFIGURABLE: corePoolSize (always running), maximumPoolSize (upper limit), queueCapacity (buffer), rejectionPolicy (AbortPolicy throws exception, CallerRunsPolicy runs on submitter's thread). SIZING: CPU-bound tasks: threads = num_cores. I/O-bound tasks: threads = num_cores × (1 + wait_time/compute_time). If compute=5ms, wait=50ms: threads = 8 × (1+10) = 88.

Single thread runs an event loop that multiplexes I/O across many connections. Used by: Node.js, Redis, NGINX, Netty. HOW: one thread calls epoll_wait() → gets list of ready sockets → processes each → loops. Non-blocking I/O: if an operation would block (disk read, network write), register a callback and continue processing other events. The callback is invoked when the operation completes. ADVANTAGE: handles thousands of concurrent connections with one thread (no context switching overhead). DISADVANTAGE: CPU-bound work blocks the entire event loop. FIX: offload CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a thread pool.

Two or more threads are waiting for each other to release locks, creating a cycle. Four necessary conditions (Coffman): (1) Mutual Exclusion: resource held exclusively. (2) Hold and Wait: thread holds one lock while waiting for another. (3) No Preemption: locks can't be forcibly taken. (4) Circular Wait: thread A waits for B, B waits for A. PREVENTION: break any one condition. Lock ordering: always acquire locks in a fixed global order (by lock ID). Breaks circular wait. Timeout: tryLock(timeout) — give up after N ms. Breaks hold-and-wait. DETECTION: build a wait-for graph (nodes = threads, edge = A waits for B's lock). If the graph has a cycle, deadlock exists. Kill one thread in the cycle (victim selection).

chapters.title: Rate Limiting
chapters.summary: Rate limiting algorithms with internals — Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed/Sliding Window — distributed rate limiting, and response headers.

explanation.overview: Rate limiting controls the number of requests a client can make in a time window. It protects your system from abuse (DDoS), ensures fair usage among clients, prevents resource exhaustion, and enforces billing tiers. Every production API has rate limiting — typically implemented at the API Gateway or Load Balancer layer.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: A bucket holds up to C tokens (capacity). Tokens are added at rate R per second. Each request consumes 1 token. If bucket is empty, request is rejected (429 Too Many Requests). IMPLEMENTATION: don't run a timer to add tokens. Instead, compute tokens lazily: on each request, calculate tokens_available = min(C, stored_tokens + R × (now - last_refill_time)). If tokens_available >= 1, allow and decrement. Store: {tokens: float, last_refill: timestamp}. In Redis: two keys per client (tokens + last_refill), updated atomically with a Lua script. BEHAVIOR: allows bursts up to C tokens, then sustains at rate R. Example: C=10, R=2/sec. A client can burst 10 requests instantly, then 2/sec thereafter. CONFIGURABLE: C controls burst size. R controls sustained rate. Different buckets for different endpoints (/api = 100/min, /search = 20/min). USED BY: AWS API Gateway, Stripe, GitHub API.

INTERNAL: requests enter a queue (bucket). The queue drains at a fixed rate R. If the queue is full (capacity C), new requests are dropped. Unlike token bucket, leaky bucket smooths output — no bursts. Output rate is always exactly R, regardless of how bursty the input is. IMPLEMENTATION: use a FIFO queue. A scheduler dequeues and processes at rate R. If queue.size >= C, reject. USE WHEN: you need a perfectly smooth request rate (bandwidth shaping, network traffic policing).

INTERNAL: divide time into fixed windows (60-second intervals). Each window has a counter starting at 0. Each request increments the counter. If counter > limit, reject. At window boundary, counter resets. IMPLEMENTATION (Redis): key = rate_limit:{client_id}:{window_start}. INCR key, EXPIRE key 60. Very simple, O(1) per request. PROBLEM: boundary burst — a client can send limit requests at 00:59 and limit requests at 01:00, effectively getting 2× limit in a 1-second window. FIX: sliding window.

INTERNAL: store the timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis ZADD). On each request: remove entries older than window_size ago (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), count remaining entries (ZCARD), if count < limit, add current timestamp (ZADD). ACCURATE: no boundary issues. EXPENSIVE: stores one entry per request. 1000 requests/minute × 1M users = 1B entries. Too much memory. USE: when accuracy matters and traffic is low.

INTERNAL: combines fixed window with weighted averaging. Keep counters for current window and previous window. Estimated count = prev_window_count × overlap_percentage + curr_window_count. Example: 60-second windows. We're 15 seconds into the current window. Previous window had 45 requests. Current window has 18 requests. Estimated rate = 45 × (45/60) + 18 = 45 × 0.75 + 18 = 33.75 + 18 = 51.75. If limit is 60, allow. IMPLEMENTATION: just two counters (2 Redis keys per client). O(1) memory. Error < 0.003% in practice. USED BY: Cloudflare for their rate limiting. This is the industry-standard algorithm — simple, memory-efficient, and accurate enough.

advanced_tweaks.how: Rate limit by: IP address (100 req/min per IP), API key (1000 req/min per key), user ID (50 req/min per user), endpoint (/login has stricter limit). A single request must pass ALL rate limits.

Instead of hard blocking at limit, degrade gradually: 0-80% of limit = full speed. 80-100% = add artificial delay (100-500ms). 100%+ = return 429. This gives the client a chance to back off before being hard-blocked.

key_concepts.definition: All rate limit state in Redis. Every request checks Redis via Lua script (atomic INCR + EXPIRE). PROS: accurate (single source of truth, no over-allowance). CONS: Redis is a SPOF for rate limiting (if Redis is down, do you allow all or deny all?). Added latency (~0.5ms per request). FIX for SPOF: fail open (allow all requests if Redis is down) for most APIs. Fail closed (block all) for critical endpoints (payment, login).

Each app server maintains local rate limit counters. Periodically sync with central store (every 1-5 seconds). Between syncs, each server allows limit/num_servers requests. PROS: no single point of failure, no per-request latency to Redis. CONS: allows slight over-limit (up to num_servers × overage_per_server). Acceptable for most use cases — rate limits are soft boundaries.

Always return rate limit info in response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 (max requests per window), X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42 (requests left in current window), X-RateLimit-Reset: 1710456789 (Unix timestamp when window resets), Retry-After: 30 (seconds to wait, included with 429 response).
